sn42.8:1.6: This saying echoes Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.5.1.4–5, but appears to misrepresent the Jain text. There, Mahāvīra says a person who “relentlessly kills movable and immovable beings for the sake of his own comfort, who injures them, who takes what is not freely given, who does not train at all in what is to be cultivated, the impudent sinner who, unsated, injures many beings will go to hell” (translation adapted from Jacobi). The closeness of the two passages is shown by the form: the first phrase speaks of the ill deeds that are done, while the second phrase in both cases uses the word _bahuṇa_/_bahula_, “frequently, repeatedly, usually”. The use of “relentlessly” (_tivva_, Pali _tibba_, Sanskrit _tīrva_) implies a violent and excessive action. As quoted in the Pali, the first phrase of Mahāvīra’s view suggests that anyone at all who kills will go to hell. This sense is conveyed through the emphatic distributive pronoun _yo koci_ (“everyone who”), whereas the Jain text has the unemphatic _je_ (“one who”). The Jain text restricts the distributive to one who does not train “at all” (_kiṁci_). Thus the thrust of the Jain passage is that one who frequently kills for their own pleasure, without even trying to do better, will go to hell. The sense of the Pali passage is both more severe and less coherent, as the first phrase implies that any killer goes to hell, while the second speaks of habitual action.
sn42.8:7.6: The following passage shows a healthy response to one’s own ethical lapses, lost neither in guilt nor in denial, but acknowledging the mistake and determining to do better.
